We all have that one person…

that person that is always doing too much.

"Over sabi."

If you’re Yoruba, you already understand that word 😅

That one person in the family, any small occasion… they are everywhere. Carrying chairs, giving instructions, talking, moving up and down like they are in charge of everything.

Or that person back in school…

once the teacher asks a question, their hand is already up.

Not just answering… they’ll explain, add extra, go off point, come back again.

Even in exams, they are always collecting extra sheets.

And when they leave the room…

you already know what people start saying.

“That one too dey do.”

Now pause.

That right there… is branding.

Not logo.
Not colors.
Not your bio.

What people are saying when you’re not in the room.

That’s your brand.

Because whether you like it or not, people are forming an opinion about you.

From how you talk.
From how you show up.
From how you behave.

So the real question is…

what are people saying about you?

Are you the one that is always doing too much?

Are you the one that doesn’t listen?

Are you the one that just wants to be seen?

Or are you the one that people actually respect when you speak?

Because you don’t even need to talk too much before people pay attention.

Now think about this…

Elon Musk is known for thinking ahead and doing things that look strange at first… so when anything comes out of his companies, people expect something different.

Aliko Dangote is known for business dominance… so when he enters any industry, people already believe he’s going to take over.

Mark Zuckerberg is known for building and controlling platforms… so when he touches anything social, people expect scale.

That didn’t start today.

It was built over time.

So again…

who are you?

And more importantly…

what are people saying about you when you’re not there?

Because whether you’re intentional about it or not…you already have a brand.

One thing I’ve learnt after 16 yrs in sales and 11 yrs in business is this..

Your reputation & prior actions follow you longer than you think.

I had a conversation yesterday where someone asked me if I’d ever do business with a certain business owner.

My answer was immediately NO.

Not because of one single event.
My gut just said no.
And over time, I’d seen enough patterns to trust that feeling.

They then shared that someone close to them eventually got badly burned by that exact company.

That’s the thing about patterns, they leave clues.

Professionally.
Personally.
In business.
In friendships.
In relationships.

From the inside, people think they’re hiding it well.

But from the outside?
The patterns are often painfully obvious.

People are ALWAYS watching.
Not just what you say, but how you move.

What you post.
What you don’t post.
How you treat people when there’s nothing to gain.
The stories that constantly follow you (there's no smoke without fire as they say).

And the crazy part is this...
you may never even know your name came up in conversation.

People talk over coffee.
Over dinner.
In business meetings.
In mutual circles.

The world is a very small place.

A lot of people think they’re controlling the narrative online.
They think people can’t see through it.

But we live in the most sophisticated consumer generation there’s ever been.

People eventually see through fake integrity.
Fake success.
Fake humility.
Fake values.

And eventually, it catches up.

You may get the instant 'fix' or dopamine hit.
You may get financial or emotional gain, but very rarely have I seen these people have true fulfilment. 

As I always say:
You can’t see the label when you’re inside the bottle.

But from the outside?
The label is obvious.

So think carefully about the things you do today.

Because whether you realise it or not, you’re building a reputation your future self will either thank you for, or spend years trying to escape.

🚪 „Man lernt sich immer zweimal kennen: beim Einstieg und beim Ausstieg.“
Ein wunderbares Zitat, das @maschmeyer vor kurzem in einem Gespräch erwähnte. Der erste Eindruck zählt aber der letzte bleibt. ✨

Genau hier wird es spannend: Wie professionell verhalten wir uns, wenn es unbequem wird?

Ich erlebe es immer wieder, dass beim Exit plötzlich alle Brücken abgebrochen werden. Oft aus Emotion oder Trotz, aber fast immer kurzsichtig:
👉 Das Arbeitszeugnis wird heimlich bei HR angefordert, ohne ein Wort an die Führungskraft.
👉 Nach der Kündigung folgt die „kollektive Krankschreibung“ bis zum letzten Tag.
👉 Wissen wird nicht mehr geteilt („Sollen sie sehen, wie sie klarkommen.“).
👉 Projekte werden einfach liegengelassen statt sauber übergeben.

Professionalität zeigt sich, wenn es schwierig wird. 💼
Ja, es gibt schlechte Führung und Enttäuschungen. Aber ein sauberer, respektvoller Exit ist kein Geschenk an das Unternehmen. Es ist eine Investition in die eigene Reputation.

Die Arbeitswelt ist verdammt klein. Und man begegnet sich tatsächlich immer zweimal im Leben. 🔄

Meine klare Haltung:
Brücken abbrennen ist kein Zeichen von Stärke, sondern ein Mangel an Weitsicht. Wer Haltung zeigt, geht auch dann souverän, wenn es innerlich brodelt. Dein letzter Eindruck ist Deine nachhaltigste Visitenkarte! 📇

People don't always judge you on truth. They judge you on what feels true. That's a reputation problem worth understanding.

The brain craves certainty. When it finds an explanation that reduces discomfort and closes the loop, it stops looking, even if that explanation is wrong, incomplete or unfair to you.

That premature conclusion becomes the story someone tells about you, and often, the story they protect.

That's not cynicism. It's psychology. And knowing it can change how you think about your reputation, your relationships and the judgments you've had to carry that you never deserved.
